**June 23, 1956 — a Saturday**

You were born in the middle of a summer that was quietly remaking the world, in ways most people wouldn't fully understand until autumn.

---

**On the exact day you were born**, Egyptians went to the polls in a constitutional referendum that confirmed Gamal Abdel Nasser as President of Egypt. It was an overwhelming endorsement — and the formal consolidation of power for a leader who was about to do something no Arab government had dared. Thirty-three days later, on July 26, Nasser announced the nationalization of the Suez Canal. Britain and France were furious; Israel invaded in October; the United States forced a humiliating withdrawal from all three. The Suez Crisis effectively ended British and French imperial authority in the Middle East, shifted the balance of Cold War influence, and made Nasser the most celebrated leader in the Arab world. All of that cascaded from the political moment that coincided with your birth.

---

**Six days after you were born**, on June 29, President Eisenhower signed the Federal Aid Highway Act — the legislation creating the Interstate Highway System. Forty-one thousand miles of limited-access highway, the largest public works project in American history. It would reshape where people lived, how cities grew, what industries survived, and what the country looked like from above. You entered a world where the highway system didn't exist yet. By the time you were in grade school, it was already changing everything.

---

**The summer you were born into** had a particular charge beneath its surface.

Four months earlier, in February, Soviet Premier Khrushchev had delivered his "Secret Speech" to the 20th Party Congress — a shocking internal denunciation of Stalin's crimes, purges, and cult of personality. The speech was supposed to be confidential. It leaked. By June 1956, it was ricocheting through the Eastern bloc, delegitimizing communist orthodoxy in ways the Kremlin hadn't anticipated. Four months after your birth, Hungary would erupt in revolt. Soviet tanks would crush it by November. The Cold War's "peaceful coexistence" period was already fracturing.

Meanwhile in Montgomery, Alabama, the bus boycott was in its seventh month. Rosa Parks had refused to give up her seat in December 1955; the legal challenge was winding through the courts; the Black community of Montgomery was still walking. The boycott would succeed in December 1956, and the movement's momentum — and its young leader, Martin Luther King Jr., then 27 — would keep building for the next decade.

---

And then there was **rock and roll**. "Heartbreak Hotel" had hit number one in April. Elvis Presley was 21 years old. You were born in the first year rock and roll became genuinely mass — not a subculture, not a novelty, but the sound a generation was deciding to claim. You didn't grow up hearing it arrive; you grew up *inside* it, from the beginning.

---

**The arc of 70 years**

You are 70 years old this year. Think about what that span contains.

You were one year old when Sputnik went up and the Space Age began. You were seven when Kennedy was shot — old enough to remember the day. You were thirteen when Neil Armstrong stepped onto the moon, and still thirteen when Woodstock happened the same summer. You came of age during Vietnam and Watergate, the two events that most corroded American institutional trust in the 20th century. You were 30 when Chernobyl burned and 33 when the Berlin Wall came down — that last one still not entirely believable, even in retrospect.

You entered the workforce before personal computers were common, navigated the internet's arrival in mid-career, and watched the smartphone remake social life after 50. You were 45 on September 11, 2001.

The Egypt you were born alongside — the one Nasser was leading toward confrontation with European imperialism — is now in its fifth republic. The Interstate System you were born days before has needed major repair for decades. The Cold War that defined your entire childhood and young adulthood ended before you turned 40.

You entered a world of newsprint, rotary phones, and no highway system yet. Seventy years later, the infrastructure of daily life has been rebuilt, more than once, entirely around you.
